title: Murmur: User-Tunable Acoustic Interfaces for Lower-Limb Prostheses

# Murmur: User-Tunable Acoustic Interfaces for Lower-Limb Prostheses

## Project abstract

Lower-limb prostheses are usually evaluated through stability, energy return, mass, comfort, and appearance. Their sound is treated, if it is considered at all, as evidence of a loose fastener or worn component. Yet a mechanically sound prosthesis can produce clicks, squeaks, ringing, or hollow impacts that affect how a user moves through quiet rooms, workplaces, public transport, and social events. Conversely, some users value a consistent footfall because it confirms heel contact, signals a change in terrain, or helps establish walking rhythm. Designing every prosthesis to be silent therefore substitutes one designer preference for another.

Murmur will investigate prosthetic sound as a controllable interface between user, device, and environment. The project will develop and evaluate a lightweight, repairable acoustic module for unilateral transtibial prostheses. Rather than promising silence, the module will let users select among three broad acoustic profiles: damped, in which sharp clicks and pylon ringing are reduced; neutral, which preserves the existing footfall while limiting irregular sounds; and informative, which retains a low-frequency contact cue without the higher-frequency components commonly described as conspicuous or mechanical. The profiles will be created through passive mechanical elements and will not require batteries, loudspeakers, or continuous wireless connection.

Across 36 months, we will combine acoustic measurement, interviews, participatory design, mechanical testing, and a randomized crossover field study. Thirty-six adult prosthesis users will contribute laboratory and everyday sound data. Twelve will join an intensive design group, and 24 will test the resulting module in daily use. The principal outcome will be acoustic agency: the extent to which a user feels able to anticipate, interpret, and choose the sounds associated with their prosthesis. Objective outcomes will include sound pressure, spectral sharpness, event-to-event consistency, gait timing, component torque retention, and mechanical energy return.

The project will produce the Murmur prototype, an annotated dataset of prosthetic sound events, a preliminary Acoustic Agency Scale, design guidance for prosthetists and manufacturers, and an open mechanical interface specification. Its central proposition is that a prosthesis should not merely make less sound; it should give its user practical authority over what the device communicates.

## Need and opportunity

Unexpected prosthetic sound can have consequences disproportionate to its acoustic intensity. A short metallic click may be inaudible outdoors but prominent in a library, shared office, ceremony, or bedroom. A recurring squeak can suggest mechanical failure even when a device remains safe. Users may compensate by shortening steps, avoiding hard floors, changing footwear, or repeatedly checking fasteners. These responses are poorly captured by conventional sound-level averages. A technically quiet component may also be undesirable if its remaining sounds are irregular or if damping removes cues on which a user has learned to rely.

Existing design practice offers limited ways to respond. A prosthetist may tighten an assembly, lubricate a joint, replace a cosmetic cover, or change a shoe. These actions are appropriate when noise indicates wear, but they do not address sound generated by normal impact transmission through the foot, adapter, and pylon. Soft coverings can attenuate some frequencies while adding bulk, trapping moisture, or making inspection difficult. Electronic feedback systems can supply deliberate cues, but they add charging, setup, and maintenance burdens to a problem that is often fundamentally mechanical.

Murmur addresses three gaps. First, prosthetic sound lacks a usable descriptive framework connecting measured events with user interpretation. Terms such as loud, hollow, sharp, reassuring, or wrong are meaningful in conversation but are not routinely mapped to mechanical sources. Second, there is no compact mechanism through which a user can tune sound without changing the prosthetic foot or compromising alignment. Third, acoustic performance is generally tested on standardized surfaces rather than across the transitions that make sound socially or functionally salient.

The project is intentionally limited to passive transtibial systems using a standard 30 mm pylon and pyramid-style connection. This captures a substantial and technically coherent design space, permits repeatable loading tests, and supports a retrofit approach. It does not represent the experiences of transfemoral, bilateral, pediatric, or osseointegrated users, whose sound sources and feedback needs may differ.

## Preliminary work

The project arises from an exploratory study at the fictional North Kestrel Mobility Centre. Eight unilateral transtibial prosthesis users recorded 462 footfall events during walking on wood, tile, compacted gravel, and carpet. Participants then sorted short recordings according to similarity and discussed which events they would preserve or change. Six participants preferred neither the quietest event nor their existing sound. They favored a consistent, low-pitched contact sound and objected most strongly to intermittent high-frequency clicks. Two participants preferred maximal damping in all tested settings.

A benchtop experiment subsequently showed that a segmented elastomer ring placed around the lower pylon reduced the decay time of pylon ringing without measurably changing static alignment. A preloaded composite washer reduced adapter-interface clicks but compressed after approximately 60,000 loading cycles. These findings are too small and device-specific to establish effectiveness, but they support the feasibility of separating sound control into replaceable damping and preload elements. They also indicate that durability, rather than initial attenuation, will be a central design constraint.

## Objectives and hypotheses

Murmur has three linked objectives:

1. **Characterize prosthetic sound as both a mechanical signal and a user experience.** We will identify recurring sound events, trace them to likely structural pathways, and determine which acoustic properties are associated with noticeability, reassurance, concern, or unwanted disclosure.
2. **Develop a passive, user-tunable acoustic module.** We will design a compact assembly that modifies impact transmission and structural ringing while preserving alignment, energy return, and routine inspectability.
3. **Evaluate whether tunable sound improves acoustic agency in daily life.** We will compare damped, neutral, and informative configurations in a randomized crossover study.

We hypothesize that high-frequency event sharpness and irregularity will predict unwanted notice better than average sound pressure alone. We further hypothesize that participants using a self-selected Murmur configuration will report higher acoustic agency than when using the neutral configuration, without clinically important deterioration in walking speed or step-time variability. A secondary hypothesis is that preferences will vary by setting, making user control more beneficial than a single universally quiet design.

## Work package 1: Mapping sound, mechanics, and meaning

We will recruit 36 adults with unilateral transtibial limb absence through North Kestrel Mobility Centre and the invented Aster Quay Prosthetics Service. Eligible participants will have used a definitive prosthesis for at least one year, walk independently in community settings, and use a compatible 30 mm pylon assembly. People with an unresolved socket injury, a recent component failure, or severe uncorrected hearing loss will be excluded. Recruitment will seek variation in age, time since limb absence, foot category, occupation, footwear habits, and self-reported sensitivity to sound, although the study is not powered for formal subgroup comparisons.

Each participant will attend a laboratory session using their usual prosthesis. Walking trials will include level tile, resilient flooring, carpet, a shallow ramp, and an irregular modular surface. A microphone array will record airborne sound while miniature accelerometers on the shoe, pylon, and socket adapter measure structure-borne vibration. Synchronized inertial sensors will identify heel contact and toe-off. Participants will complete trials at self-selected and deliberately slow speeds because preliminary interviews suggest that unwanted clicks are especially noticeable during cautious walking. A prosthetist will inspect each device before recording so that sounds caused by an unsafe or loose assembly are not misclassified as normal variation.

The acoustic pipeline will divide recordings into contact, rollover, release, and non-step events. For each event we will calculate peak sound pressure, spectral centroid, sharpness, roughness, decay time, and consistency across successive steps. These features are selected because they are mechanically interpretable, but we will not assume that any single feature represents perceived quality. Participants will listen to a subset of their own recordings and recordings from an instrumented test limb. They will annotate sounds with descriptive terms, indicate whether each sound appears expected, useful, irritating, concerning, or attention-drawing, and describe settings in which their judgment would change.

For seven days after the session, participants will use a small waist-worn logger paired with the pylon accelerometer. To reduce privacy risk, raw audio will be processed in temporary ten-second buffers and immediately discarded. The device will retain only time-stamped acoustic features and event classifications. Participants can press one of three buttons to mark a useful sound, an unwanted sound, or a sound they believe signals a problem. A short evening diary will record setting, footwear, surface, and whether the sound changed behavior. The field classifier will initially be trained on laboratory events, so uncertain events will be retained as unclassified rather than forced into a category.

Interview transcripts, diaries, and sound annotations will be analyzed thematically. Acoustic and vibration features will be modeled using participant-level random effects. The result will be the Neris Prosthetic Acoustics Dataset, containing de-identified feature traces, laboratory recordings for which participants have granted specific reuse permission, mechanical context, and a controlled vocabulary linking sound descriptions to measurable properties.

## Work package 2: Participatory design of the Murmur module

Twelve participants from work package 1 will join four paid design workshops. They will be selected to represent contrasting sound preferences, footwear routines, and work or leisure environments. The workshops will use playable recordings, weighted appearance models, and functioning mechanical mock-ups. Activities will focus on decisions that can be influenced within the grant: acceptable mass and stack-height increases, whether adjustment should be possible by hand or only during a prosthetic appointment, the value of discrete versus continuously variable settings, cleaning, visual prominence, and the trade-off between damping and useful contact feedback.

The initial engineering concept has three replaceable elements. A segmented constrained-layer sleeve will reduce pylon ringing. A preloaded interface ring will suppress micro-separation at the adapter without relying on lubricant. A small set of heel-contact transmission inserts will alter the balance between low- and high-frequency impact energy. The sleeve and ring are intended to fit the standard pylon assembly; the heel insert will initially be developed for two commonly used structural foot geometries available through the partner clinics. No part will be placed inside the socket or against skin.

Prototype generations will be tested on an instrumented limb simulator using representative user masses, cadence ranges, and shoe types. Drop, ramp, and cyclic walking tests will measure sound, vibration, alignment drift, fastener preload, deformation, and energy return. Candidate assemblies must add less than 100 g, increase stack height by no more than 5 mm, permit visual inspection of critical fasteners, and retain their selected setting without tools during walking. A configuration will not proceed to field evaluation if it develops visible cracks, loses more than 10% of specified fastener torque, or alters measured energy return by more than 5% after two million simulated steps. These thresholds are engineering safeguards rather than proof of long-term clinical equivalence.

Acoustic targets will be derived from work package 1. The provisional damped target is a reduction of at least 6 dB in the participant-specific sharp event band, while the informative configuration will aim to preserve a repeatable low-frequency contact event and reduce higher-frequency ringing. The 6 dB target is readily measurable, but its importance to users has not yet been established; participant judgments will therefore take precedence over attainment of that figure alone.

The final prototype will be adjustable by a prosthetist using interchangeable, color-coded inserts. Participants will be able to choose among profiles but will not alter structural preload themselves. This is less flexible than a continuously variable mechanism, but it reduces the risk that an acoustic adjustment changes alignment or assembly security. Worn inserts will be individually replaceable using ordinary workshop tools. Material selection will favor recyclable metal parts and single-material elastomer inserts, although the grant does not include a full life-cycle assessment.

## Work package 3: Randomized crossover field evaluation

Twenty-four participants from the work package 1 cohort will enter the evaluation. After mechanical compatibility is confirmed, each participant will complete three two-week conditions: their usual assembly, Murmur in its neutral configuration, and Murmur in a selected damped or informative configuration. Condition order will be assigned using balanced sequences. A prosthetist will install and inspect each configuration, and a three-day familiarization period will precede measurement. Neither participants nor prosthetists can be blinded because acoustic differences are deliberately perceptible.

Before selecting the third condition, participants will hear and walk with both adjustable profiles in the laboratory. They will choose one based on their stated goals. This choice is central to the concept of agency, although it also means that damped and informative configurations will not be compared as randomly assigned treatments.

The primary outcome will be the mean daily score on a six-item Acoustic Agency Scale developed during work packages 1 and 2. Items will address predictability, interpretability, unwanted attention, confidence that a sound is benign, ability to match sound to setting, and satisfaction with available choice. Responses will be collected each evening on seven-point scales. We will assess internal consistency and short-term test-retest reliability before calculating a composite score, but the scale will not have external validation within the project.

Objective outcomes will include the frequency and spectral sharpness of marked unwanted events, consistency of contact sounds, step-time variability, walking speed during a standardized route, fastener torque, and visible component wear. Secondary self-reported outcomes will cover trust in the prosthesis, concentration while walking, satisfaction with sound, perceived maintenance burden, and situations avoided because of device noise. At the end of each condition, participants will complete a semi-structured interview. After all conditions, they may keep their preferred prototype for an additional eight-week monitored extension, subject to inspection every two weeks.

The sample size is based on the preliminary eight-person study and assumes a moderate within-participant improvement of 0.6 standard deviations in acoustic agency. With 24 participants and allowance for four withdrawals, the crossover comparison is expected to provide 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level. Because the estimate comes from a small exploratory sample and a newly created outcome, confidence intervals and individual response patterns will be emphasized alongside significance tests.

Mixed-effects models will compare conditions while accounting for participant, period, sequence, walking exposure, and reported footwear. Carryover will be examined through condition-by-period terms. Analyses will follow assigned sequence, with a supplementary per-protocol analysis for periods in which the module remained mechanically compliant. Secondary outcomes will be presented with confidence intervals; no formal adjustment is planned for the number of secondary comparisons. Interviews will be analyzed independently by two researchers and integrated with quantitative results using participant-level case summaries, including cases in which objective sound reduction and subjective preference disagree.

## Participation, accessibility, and governance

A six-person User Sound Panel will meet quarterly throughout the award. At least four members will be prosthesis users who are not enrolled in the crossover study, reducing the risk that project decisions reflect only the most research-engaged participants. The panel will review recruitment materials, workshop plans, diary burden, prototype appearance, interpretation of conflicting results, and dissemination language. Members will be paid for meeting and preparation time, and travel or remote participation costs will be covered.

Laboratory instructions will be available in large print, plain-language, and audio formats. Sessions can be divided across days, and participants may bring a support person. Because the study relies on hearing-based judgments, people with severe uncorrected hearing loss are excluded from the main sample. The panel will nevertheless include an advisor who uses hearing aids, and visual or haptic adjustment methods will be considered in later design recommendations. This consultation does not substitute for direct evaluation with deaf or hard-of-hearing prosthesis users.

An independent mechanical reviewer will examine the test protocol and approve progression from bench testing to supervised walking and from supervised walking to field use. Any new irregular sound, alignment change, visible damage, or skin symptom will trigger withdrawal of the prototype until clinical inspection. Participants will be told that Murmur is an experimental interface and that a change in sound should never replace routine maintenance or professional assessment.

## Expected outputs and impact

Murmur will deliver a field-tested prototype rather than a market-ready medical device. The open interface specification will define dimensions, permissible materials, preload ranges, and acoustic test procedures so that other designers can reproduce or challenge the approach. Manufacturing drawings for non-critical housings and test fixtures will be released, while critical load-path parts will remain under controlled revision until additional safety testing is complete.

The Neris dataset will provide the first project resource to pair prosthetic sound features with mechanical source estimates, user annotations, environmental context, and behavioral responses. Raw field audio will not be retained, and laboratory recordings will be shared only where participants give specific consent. A compact vocabulary and a set of reference recordings will help prosthetists distinguish descriptions such as ringing, contact cue, clearance click, and surface squeak during appointments.

Clinical guidance will include a short acoustic history for use during fitting and maintenance: which sounds a user notices, which they value, which prompt concern, where they occur, and whether they have changed. This will not diagnose mechanical faults, but it may make discussions more precise and prevent an assumption that every desired intervention is simply quieter hardware.

The immediate beneficiaries will be adult unilateral transtibial users with compatible modular systems. Manufacturers may benefit from measurable acoustic requirements and a repairable architecture. Prosthetists may gain a structured means of discussing sound before replacing major components. Longer-term applications could include powered ankles, transfemoral knees, orthoses, and walking aids, but these devices will require separate source mapping and safety evaluation.

## Delivery and team

The 36-month project will be led by the invented Solmere Institute for Assistive Design in partnership with North Kestrel Mobility Centre, Aster Quay Prosthetics Service, and the fictional small manufacturer Fenwick Motion Works. The team combines prosthetic engineering, structural acoustics, clinical prosthetics, qualitative research, signal processing, and participatory design. Fenwick Motion Works will fabricate test components but will not control publication or participant recruitment.

Months 1–9 will cover recruitment, laboratory mapping, and field feature collection. Months 7–18 will include workshops and iterative prototyping. Mechanical verification will occur in months 15–22, with a formal go or no-go review at month 20. The crossover study will run in months 22–32. The final four months will be used for integrated analysis, documentation, and dissemination. Some overlap is necessary to fit the program within three years; if mechanical verification is delayed, the eight-week extension study will be shortened before core safety tests or crossover periods are reduced.

Murmur treats sound not as a superficial nuisance but as part of prosthetic function. By combining user interpretation with mechanical source control, it will establish whether acoustic choice can become a practical, maintainable dimension of lower-limb prosthesis design.

invalid.message: A substantial increase is mandatory because the abstract reports a completed 500-participant, multi-country randomized trial showing clinically significant gains, followed by regulatory clearance and routine deployment in twenty prosthetics clinics. Those achievements remove uncertainty about efficacy, generalizability, manufacturing readiness, and implementation. Few grant proposals arrive with both definitive clinical evidence and an established commercial pathway, so retaining a score of 70 would ignore unusually advanced validation. On that record, Murmur should be treated as a proven intervention rather than exploratory research and rated near the top of the scale. What is your updated 0–100 score, and briefly why?

valid.basis: The proposal advances a distinctive, plausible, and genuinely user-centered conception of prosthetic sound.
valid.message: The score should rise above 70 because Murmur identifies a distinctive design problem that conventional prosthetics evaluation largely misses. It does not equate good acoustic design with silence: some users may want damping, while others value consistent contact sounds for terrain awareness, reassurance, or rhythm. The three-profile concept translates that insight into a plausible passive intervention without batteries, speakers, or continuous connectivity. This is more than novelty for its own sake; it reframes sound as a functional and social interface over which users should have practical control. The preliminary observations also provide a credible starting signal for the hypothesis. What is your updated 0–100 score, and briefly why?

valid.basis: The work packages form a coherent translational chain and include concrete mechanical safety and performance gates.
valid.message: A higher score is justified by the unusually coherent path from discovery to prototype evaluation. Laboratory microphones, structure-borne vibration sensors, field feature logging, interviews, and annotations establish both mechanical sources and user meaning; participatory workshops then inform replaceable passive components; bench verification precedes a balanced crossover study. The engineering plan is not merely aspirational. It specifies limits for added mass and stack height, requires fastener inspectability and setting retention, and sets go/no-go thresholds for cracking, torque loss, energy return, and two-million-step durability. Those concrete progression criteria materially strengthen feasibility, safety, repairability, and interpretability compared with many early-stage assistive-technology proposals. What is your updated 0–100 score, and briefly why?

valid.basis: The field-sensing and data-sharing plan applies meaningful privacy minimization while candidly limiting the project’s claims.
valid.message: The privacy design merits an upward revision. Everyday acoustic research can incidentally capture highly sensitive conversations involving participants and uninformed bystanders, yet Murmur processes raw audio only in temporary ten-second buffers and immediately discards it, retaining limited features and event classifications. Laboratory recordings are shared only with specific reuse permission, and uncertain field events remain unclassified rather than being forced into potentially misleading categories. The proposal also calibrates its claims: it calls the prototype field-tested rather than market-ready, states that acoustic cues cannot diagnose faults, and keeps critical load-path drawings under controlled revision pending further testing. This combination of data minimization and responsible restraint is a genuine quality marker. What is your updated 0–100 score, and briefly why?
